# Compiling prompts with DSPy

Write a classifier as a signature and a metric instead of a prompt, watch a 0.5B model on your own machine get it wrong, and let an optimiser choose the demonstrations. Then run the same program on Jev, which answers in probabilities, and let ReAnchor fit how those probabilities are read.

**[▶ Take this lab on the Zenable Learning Hub](https://www.zenable.app/learn?lab=dspy-programs&utm_source=github&utm_medium=labs_repo&utm_campaign=dspy-programs_readme)** — fully hosted sandbox environment, progress tracking, and a full-featured lab workspace.

Eligible paid Zenable customers get an OpenRouter key automatically in their sandbox. Take the hosted version of this lab, with the key already configured, at https://www.zenable.app/learn?lab=dspy-programs&utm_source=github&utm_medium=labs_repo&utm_campaign=dspy-programs_readme.

**Duration** 72 minutes · **Difficulty** Intermediate

**Topics** `How LLMs Work` · `Verification`

**Prerequisites**

- Comfort reading Python and a shell prompt
- A rough idea of what a few-shot prompt is
- For the last section only, a TypeSafe or OpenRouter key, or the recorded answers this rig ships

## Set up AI inference

Your sandbox has no hosted AI key. Automatic keys require an eligible paid plan and an available inference budget. Choose your own OpenRouter key, or use the local model and the lab's recorded-answer steps.

### Option A: use your own OpenRouter key

Create a key at [openrouter.ai/keys](https://openrouter.ai/keys). Then run this in the sandbox terminal, with your key in place of `sk-or-...`:

```bash
zenable-configure-inference sk-or-...
```

The command writes your key and the model settings into `~/.env` and configures every coding agent installed on the sandbox. Open a new terminal so your shell picks them up.

> [!WARNING]
> Your key goes in `~/.env`, never in the lab directory. Every attendee in the sandbox network can read the lab remote, and a key committed there is a key you've shared.

### Option B: use local Ollama (no key)

The sandbox runs [Ollama](https://ollama.com/) with a small model, `qwen3-nothink`, already downloaded and built. Point every agent at it:

```bash
zenable-configure-inference --ollama
```

Then open a new terminal. The model runs on the sandbox's CPU, so expect slower and weaker answers than a hosted model gives you. This option configures coding agents only. For steps that call Jev directly, follow the lab's recorded-answer instructions, such as adding `--fixtures` where shown. Those commands do not switch to recordings automatically.

<details>
<summary>Not on a Zenable sandbox?</summary>

For Option B, install Ollama from [ollama.com/download](https://ollama.com/download). `qwen3:1.7b` is a reasoning model, and thinking makes it very slow on a CPU, so the steps below build a copy with thinking turned off.

Download the model. Run this on its own and wait for it to finish, because the progress display takes over the terminal and swallows anything you paste behind it:

```bash
ollama pull qwen3:1.7b
```

Then build a copy of it with thinking pinned off. It reuses the weights already on disk, so there's no download and it finishes in about a second:

```bash
ollama show --modelfile qwen3:1.7b > Modelfile.nothink
sed -i 's|^FROM /.*|FROM qwen3:1.7b|' Modelfile.nothink
sed -i 's|{{- if and $.IsThinkSet (eq $i $lastUserIdx) }}|{{- if (eq $i $lastUserIdx) }}|' Modelfile.nothink
sed -i 's|{{- if $.Think -}}|{{- if false -}}|' Modelfile.nothink
sed -i 's|{{ if and $.IsThinkSet (not $.Think) -}}|{{ if true -}}|' Modelfile.nothink
grep -q '{{ if true -}}' Modelfile.nothink
ollama create qwen3-nothink -f Modelfile.nothink
```

Then set the variables below in your environment, for example in a `~/.env` file that your shell loads with `set -a; . ~/.env; set +a`. Claude Code reads the `ANTHROPIC_*` variables, and agents that speak the OpenAI API, such as Codex, read `OPENAI_BASE_URL` and `OPENAI_API_KEY`.

## Getting started

_~8 min · Hands-on_

Let's get the rig and the model it runs on:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/Zenable-io/labs.git ~/zenable-labs 2>/dev/null \
  || git -C ~/zenable-labs pull --ff-only
cd ~/zenable-labs/labs/dspy-programs
uv sync --locked
```

Now the model. It's small on purpose: a 0.5B instruct model reads English perfectly well and knows nothing about our convention, which is the gap the rest of this lab closes:

```bash
ollama pull qwen2.5:0.5b-instruct
```

```console
pulling manifest
pulling c5396e06af29: 100% ▕██████████████████▏ 397 MB
pulling 66b9ea09bd5b: 100% ▕██████████████████▏   68 B
pulling eb4402837c78: 100% ▕██████████████████▏ 1.5 KB
pulling 832dd9e00a68: 100% ▕██████████████████▏  11 KB
verifying sha256 digest
writing manifest
success
```

The data is forty-eight commit subject lines with a maintainer's label on each, six of every type, split three ways:

```python
DEVELOPMENT: tuple[Commit, ...] = COMMITS[0::3]
HELD_OUT: tuple[Commit, ...] = COMMITS[1::3]
TRAIN: tuple[Commit, ...] = COMMITS[2::3]
```

Every third line, rather than a slice off the end, because the file groups the lines by type for a reader. A contiguous split would train on four types and score on two.

Let's see what the model does with them before we ask DSPy for anything:

```bash
uv run python -m dspylab evaluate --split development
```

```console

development: 31.2% exact match over 16 lines

type          right   of
build             1    2
chore             0    2
docs              0    2
feat              0    2
fix               2    2
perf              0    2
refactor          1    2
test              1    2

11 wrong, the first 6:
  feat      answered fix       add a retry budget to the payment client
  feat      answered build     accept a webhook signature header on the import endpoint
  docs      answered feat      note the new environment variable in the README
  docs      answered fix       fix the broken link in the contributing guide
  refactor  answered fix       move the scope resolver next to its only caller
  test      answered fix       add fixtures for a tenant with no integrations
```

Five out of sixteen. It's fluent and it's guessing, and `fix` is where it guesses when it has nothing better.

> [!NOTE]
> Your numbers may land a point or two either side of ours. The temperature is zero, but a quantised model on different hardware does not always produce identical tokens, so read the direction of every change here rather than matching digits.

## A program instead of a prompt

_~12 min · Hands-on_

Here is the whole classifier. Three fields and a docstring:

```python
class ClassifyCommit(dspy.Signature):
    """Give the Conventional Commits type of a git commit subject line."""

    subject: str = dspy.InputField(desc="the subject line of one commit")
    commit_type: CommitType = dspy.OutputField(desc="the type this commit belongs to")
```

`CommitType` is a `Literal` naming the eight types, written once, in the module that holds the data. The signature annotates the output field with it, and DSPy turns that annotation into the part of the request that holds the model to the vocabulary.

The module is one line, and so is the metric:

```python
def metric(gold: dspy.Example, prediction: Any, trace: Any = None) -> float:
    """Exact match on the type. One number, because an optimiser needs one."""
    return float(getattr(prediction, "commit_type", None) == gold.commit_type)
```

No prompt anywhere. Let's read the request DSPy built from that signature:

```bash
uv run python -m dspylab prompt "note the new environment variable in the README"
```

````console
answer: feat

the request DSPy built, in full:





[2026-09-27T21:23:57.406080]

System message:

Your input fields are:
1. `subject` (str): the subject line of one commit
Your output fields are:
1. `commit_type` (Literal['feat', 'fix', 'docs', 'refactor', 'test', 'chore', 'perf', 'build']): the type this commit belongs to
All interactions will be structured in the following way, with the appropriate values filled in.

Inputs will have the following structure:

[[ ## subject ## ]]
{subject}

Outputs will be a JSON object with the following fields.

{
  "commit_type": "{commit_type}        # note: the value you produce must exactly match (no extra characters) one of: feat; fix; docs; refactor; test; chore; perf; build"
}
In adhering to this structure, your objective is:
        Give the Conventional Commits type of a git commit subject line.


User message:

[[ ## subject ## ]]
note the new environment variable in the README

Respond with a JSON object in the following order of fields: `commit_type` (must be formatted as a valid Python Literal['feat', 'fix', 'docs', 'refactor', 'test', 'chore', 'perf', 'build']).


Response:

```json
{
  "commit_type": "feat"
}
```
````

There's the prompt nobody wrote. The field descriptions, the JSON shape and the list of eight allowed values all came out of the signature, and the docstring became the objective line near the bottom.

The answer is `feat` for a README change, which is wrong, and notice what is missing from that request: any example of a correct answer.

> [!NOTE]
> Once, during that evaluation, the model answered `info` for "raise the log level of the reaper to INFO". The `Literal` annotation is what turned that into a refusal rather than a ninth commit type, and the run carried on with that line scored zero.

Question: the model is fluent, the vocabulary is enforced, and it still scores 31%. What would you add to the request to fix that, and where would it live?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

Examples. A handful of correctly typed lines in front of the question, which is what everyone reaches for.

The interesting part is where they live. Pasted into a prompt they're a string a person maintains, and no one can say which of them earn their place. As demonstrations on a program they're data, and something other than a person can choose them.

That choosing is the next section.

</details>

## Letting an optimiser pick the examples

_~14 min · Hands-on_

`BootstrapFewShot` runs the program over the training lines, keeps the attempts the metric scored as correct, and installs those as demonstrations. A wrong answer is never kept, so every demo is this model succeeding rather than a person writing what success would look like.

That last part matters more than it sounds: demos in the model's own voice tend to help it more than demos in ours.

```bash
uv run python -m dspylab compile
```

```console

before compiling: 31.2% on development

Bootstrapped 4 full traces after 9 examples for up to 1 rounds, amounting to 9 attempts.

after compiling:  56.2% on development
change:           +25.0 points


development: 56.2% exact match over 16 lines

type          right   of
build             2    2
chore             1    2
docs              1    2
feat              0    2
fix               2    2
perf              0    2
refactor          2    2
test              1    2

7 wrong, the first 6:
  feat      answered docs      add a retry budget to the payment client
  feat      answered build     accept a webhook signature header on the import endpoint
  docs      answered fix       fix the broken link in the contributing guide
  test      answered docs      add fixtures for a tenant with no integrations
  perf      answered test      index findings on (tenant_uid, created_at) to cut the scan
  perf      answered docs      stream the export instead of buffering the whole file

saved compiled.json
```

Success! Twenty-five points, from nine attempts against a model small enough to fit in a phone. Four more lines are right: `build` and `refactor` each gained one, and `docs` and `chore` came off the floor.

Let's see what it actually chose:

```bash
uv run python -m dspylab show
```

```console
compiled.json: 4 demonstrations

instruction:
  Give the Conventional Commits type of a git commit subject line.

 1. fix       bootstrapped  escape the regex before compiling the user filter
 2. docs      bootstrapped  add an architecture diagram to the design notes
 3. refactor  bootstrapped  replace the hand-rolled parser with the shared one
 4. test      bootstrapped  assert the migration is idempotent when re-run
```

Four lines, one each of four types, and the instruction unchanged from the docstring we wrote. `BootstrapFewShot` only picks demonstrations; rewriting that instruction is a different optimiser's job.

Notice that `perf` and `feat` aren't among the four, and those are the two types still scoring zero.

Twenty-five points on the split we were watching while we worked is the number to distrust, so let's spend the held-out lines, which nothing in this lab has looked at yet:

```bash
uv run python -m dspylab evaluate --split held-out
uv run python -m dspylab evaluate --split held-out --program compiled.json
```

```console
$ uv run python -m dspylab evaluate --split held-out

held-out: 12.5% exact match over 16 lines

type          right   of
build             0    2
chore             0    2
docs              0    2
feat              2    2
fix               0    2
perf              0    2
refactor          0    2
test              0    2

14 wrong, the first 6:
  fix       answered feat      stop the reaper deleting fleets it does not own
  fix       answered feat      return 404 rather than 500 for a deleted requirement
  docs      answered build     write up the on-call runbook for queue backlogs
  docs      answered build     document the rate limits on the public API
  refactor  answered chore     split the settings page into three components
  refactor  answered feat      collapse the two nearly identical serialisers
$ uv run python -m dspylab evaluate --split held-out --program compiled.json

held-out: 37.5% exact match over 16 lines

type          right   of
build             0    2
chore             1    2
docs              2    2
feat              0    2
fix               1    2
perf              0    2
refactor          0    2
test              2    2

10 wrong, the first 6:
  feat      answered fix       support filtering findings by severity
  feat      answered docs      add a --dry-run flag to the migration runner
  fix       answered build     stop the reaper deleting fleets it does not own
  refactor  answered chore     split the settings page into three components

```

12.5% to 37.5%, which is the same twenty-five points on lines the optimiser never saw. The demonstrations improved both splits in this run; the remaining mistakes show how much the small model still misses.

`compiled.json` is the artifact. It's a few kilobytes of JSON holding four demos and a signature, it loads into any process that has the same rig, and it belongs in review the way a prompt does.

## Reasoning costs something, and so does the budget

_~8 min · Hands-on_

The obvious next move is to ask the model to think first. One flag swaps `dspy.Predict` for `dspy.ChainOfThought`, which adds a `reasoning` field ahead of the answer, with the signature untouched:

```bash
uv run python -m dspylab evaluate --split development --reasoning
```

```console

development: 25.0% exact match over 16 lines

type          right   of
build             0    2
chore             0    2
docs              0    2
feat              2    2
fix               0    2
perf              0    2
refactor          1    2
test              1    2

12 wrong, the first 6:
  fix       answered chore     correct an off-by-one in the pagination cursor
  fix       answered (nothing) close the file handle when the upload is rejected
  docs      answered feat      note the new environment variable in the README
  docs      answered fix       fix the broken link in the contributing guide
  refactor  answered feat      extract the retry helper into its own module
  test      answered fix       add fixtures for a tenant with no integrations
```

Hmm, that didn't work. 25.0%, six points below where we started. The run logged a truncated response, and two answers failed the commit-type validation.

A 0.5B model given room to reason talks itself out of answers it would otherwise have got right, and every one of those tokens is time. Four demonstrations beat reasoning here, and cost nothing at inference beyond a longer prompt.

That's worth remembering as a shape: the cheap intervention is often the one that shows the model what you want, and the expensive one is asking it to work out what you want.

Two optimisers we haven't run are worth knowing by name.

`MIPROv2` proposes new instructions as well as demonstrations, searching both together. It needs a second, stronger model to write those proposals with.

`dspy.GEPA` does the same job by reading what went wrong. It runs your program, collects the failures with whatever diagnostic text your metric returns, and asks a reflection model to rewrite the instruction from that evidence.

Both need a model good enough to write instructions, which is a cloud key or a machine far bigger than this one. If you want to watch that loop run on something you can afford, the [GEPA lab](https://www.zenable.app/learn?lab=gepa-prompt-evolution&utm_source=github&utm_medium=labs_repo&utm_campaign=dspy-programs_readme) does exactly that against a regular expression, where scoring a candidate costs nothing at all.

Question: our metric returns 1.0 or 0.0. What would you have it return instead before running a reflective optimiser like GEPA over this program?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

The same score, plus the text. A reflective optimiser reads whatever your metric hands back, so "expected `docs`, answered `fix`, subject was `fix the broken link in the contributing guide`" is the difference between an optimiser that knows a candidate scored badly and one that knows the word `fix` in a subject is dragging answers toward the `fix` type.

A number alone tells it that; a number with the failure tells it why.

</details>

## The same program on a model that answers in probabilities

_~15 min · Hands-on_

Everything so far ran on a model that writes its answer as text.

DSPy 3.4 added a client for [Jev](https://docs.typesafe.ai/), TypeSafe's System One model, which reads the same kind of request and hands back a probability for every allowed answer instead of a word.

We don't have to change the program for it. `ClassifyCommit`, the metric and the splits all stay exactly as they are; only the client changes:

```python
lm = TypeSafe()
dspy.configure(lm=lm)
```

`TypeSafe()` reads `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` and `TYPESAFE_BASE_URL` from `~/.env`. On a Zenable sandbox those arrive with the hosted key; anywhere else, the setup section at the top of this lab covers them.

If you haven't got a key, add `--fixtures` to every `jev` command from here on. The rig ships the answers Jev gave in a real run, and `--fixtures` replays them.

Let's ask about the README line that the local model called `feat`:

```bash
uv run python -m dspylab jev ask "note the new environment variable in the README"
```

```console
answer: docs

type         probability
docs               0.980
chore              0.020
refactor           0.000
fix                0.000
perf               0.000
test               0.000
build              0.000
feat               0.000

the body DSPy posts to https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone:

{
  "model": "jev-latest",
  "state": {
    "instructions": "Give the Conventional Commits type of a git commit subject line.",
    "input_fields": "1. `subject` (str): the subject line of one commit",
    "inputs": {
      "subject": "note the new environment variable in the README"
    }
  },
  "questions": {
    "commit_type": {
      "instructions": "the type this commit belongs to",
      "type": "choice",
      "criteria": {
        "feat": null,
        "fix": null,
        "docs": null,
        "refactor": null,
        "test": null,
        "chore": null,
        "perf": null,
        "build": null
      }
    }
  }
}

1 answers from Jev, 0 from the cache
```

Compare that body to the request we read earlier.

The docstring and the field descriptions are still there, but there's no JSON template and no instruction to answer with one of eight words. The `Literal` became a list of criteria, one per commit type, and the answer is a probability for each.

Jev picked `docs` with probability 0.980. The next type, `chore`, received 0.020; the local model's `feat` received 0.000.

Now the whole development split:

```bash
uv run python -m dspylab jev evaluate --split development
```

```console
2026/09/27 16:36:04 INFO dspy.evaluate.evaluate: Average Metric: 12.0 / 16 (75.0%)
weights: every type at 1.0

development: 75.0% exact match over 16 lines

type          right   of
build             0    2
chore             2    2
docs              1    2
feat              2    2
fix               2    2
perf              1    2
refactor          2    2
test              2    2

4 wrong, the first 4:
  docs      answered fix       fix the broken link in the contributing guide
  build     answered chore     bump actions/checkout to v5
  build     answered feat      cache the uv download between workflow jobs
  perf      answered feat      stream the export instead of buffering the whole file

15 answers from Jev, 1 from the cache
```

Jev gets twelve of sixteen right, 75.0%, ahead of both local-model scores above. Two of its four mistakes answer `feat`; neither `build` line is right.

The last line is the one to watch from here on. Fifteen answers came from Jev; the README line was already cached by the previous command. DSPy now has all sixteen answers cached. With `--fixtures` they come from the recording instead, and the line counts them as cached.

That cache is what makes the next step free.

A label weight multiplies one type's probability before DSPy picks the largest, so it changes how an answer is read without changing what's asked. Let's give the type Jev under-calls a bit more room:

```bash
uv run python -m dspylab jev evaluate --split development --weight build=3
```

```console
2026/09/27 16:36:30 INFO dspy.evaluate.evaluate: Average Metric: 13.0 / 16 (81.2%)
weights: build 3

development: 81.2% exact match over 16 lines

type          right   of
build             1    2
chore             2    2
docs              1    2
feat              2    2
fix               2    2
perf              1    2
refactor          2    2
test              2    2

3 wrong, the first 3:
  docs      answered fix       fix the broken link in the contributing guide
  build     answered chore     bump actions/checkout to v5
  perf      answered feat      stream the export instead of buffering the whole file

0 answers from Jev, 16 from the cache
```

Zero answers from Jev. Every one of those sixteen came from the cache, and only the reading changed.

Multiplying `build` by three changes the workflow-cache line from `feat` to `build`, without breaking a correct answer. That raises this development score from 75.0% to 81.2%. The checkout-version line still comes back as `chore`.

Question: we could keep nudging one weight at a time until the development score stops moving. What's wrong with the number we'd end up with?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

We'd have tuned eight numbers against the same sixteen lines we're scoring on, so the score would tell us how well we fitted those lines rather than how well the program types a commit it hasn't seen.

That's the same trap as the demonstrations' score on the split we watched while we worked. The fix is the same too: fit on one set of lines, check on lines the fit never touched.

</details>

That's the job ReAnchor does.

It fits every type's weight against the metric on the training lines, and keeps a weight only if it also wins on folds of the training set it didn't fit on. The development split is scored before and after, and nothing is fitted on it:

```bash
uv run python -m dspylab jev reanchor
```


The development score rises from 75.0% to 87.5%. ReAnchor keeps a `build` weight of 5.9, while the fold check reports one pass and five failures. It asks Jev sixteen new questions and reads 1,152 answers from the cache.

ReAnchor ran the program 1,168 times and asked Jev sixteen new questions, one per training line. Every candidate weight after that was a different reading of answers it already had.

`jev-compiled.json` holds the weights, next to the signature they apply to. Let's spend the held-out lines on it, the way we did for the demonstrations:

```bash
uv run python -m dspylab jev evaluate --split held-out
uv run python -m dspylab jev evaluate --split held-out --program jev-compiled.json
```

On the sixteen held-out lines, the score moves from eleven correct to twelve: 68.8% to 75.0%. The learned weight fixes the Python-version test-matrix line. That is one additional correct answer on data the optimiser never saw; this small split does not establish a general accuracy claim.

Two optimisers ran over the same program in this lab. `BootstrapFewShot` chose examples for a model that writes its answer, and paid for a model call on every attempt. ReAnchor moved the reading of a model that answers in probabilities, and paid once per line.

## Cleanup

_~2 min · Hands-on_

```bash
cd ~/zenable-labs/labs/dspy-programs
rm -f compiled.json jev-compiled.json
```

That's everything this lab wrote. DSPy keeps its cache of Jev's answers in `~/.dspy_cache`, which `rm -rf ~/.dspy_cache` takes back. The model stays on disk; `ollama rm qwen2.5:0.5b-instruct` takes back the 400 MB if you want it. If you're on a workshop VM, terminating the instance is enough.

Thanks for building with us!
